claims.claim: A hypothetical counterexample may be assumed to contain the empty set and to have ground set equal to the union of its members.
claims.evidence: Let m=|F| and U=⋃F. Iterated binary union closure gives U∈F, and replacing X by U merely deletes zero-frequency elements. If ∅∉F, then F∪{∅} is union-closed, has m+1 members, and preserves every frequency d_x. Thus d_x<m/2 implies d_x<(m+1)/2, so a counterexample remains a counterexample.
claims.search_method: Direct normalization proof using finite union induction and exact threshold comparison.

claims.claim: Equivalent active elements can be identified without changing the number of members or any relevant frequency.
claims.evidence: If x∼y means identical incidence columns, every member contains either an entire equivalence class or none of it. Projection onto one representative per active class therefore commutes with union. It is injective because equal projections imply equal membership for every class, hence equal original sets. Family cardinality and every representative's class frequency are consequently preserved.

claims.claim: If any counterexample exists, then a counterexample containing ∅ and having odd cardinality exists.
claims.evidence: First adjoin ∅ as in claim 0. If the resulting counterexample has even size 2k, remove a minimum-cardinality nonempty member S. No two remaining members can have union S: any nonempty operand contained in S would have size at least |S| and hence equal S. The remaining family is union-closed, and every frequency is at most k−1<(2k−1)/2. At least one nonempty member remains, since {∅,S} is not a counterexample. Its size is odd.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a singleton satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x}∈F, the map A↦A∪{x} sends members avoiding x injectively into members containing x; deleting x recovers A. Hence no more members avoid x than contain it, so d_x≥|F|/2.

claims.claim: A union-closed family containing a two-element member satisfies Frankl’s bound.
claims.evidence: For {x,y}∈F, partition F into N,X,Y,B according to whether a member contains neither, only x, only y, or both. The injection A↦A∪{x,y} gives |N|≤|B|. Therefore d_x+d_y=|X|+|Y|+2|B|=|F|+|B|−|N|≥|F|, so at least one frequency is at least |F|/2.

claims.claim: Every separating union-closed family on n active elements has an element of frequency at least n; hence it satisfies Frankl’s bound whenever |F|≤2n.
claims.evidence: Order elements by d_1≤⋯≤d_n. For i<j, separation and the frequency order imply that some member contains x_j but not x_i. Thus M_i, the union of all members avoiding x_i, belongs to F, excludes x_i, and contains x_{i+1},…,x_n. The sets M_1,…,M_{n−1} are distinct and contain x_n; the full union X is another such member. Hence d_n≥n, which is at least |F|/2 when |F|≤2n.

claims.claim: For a separating family containing ∅, an exact incidence lower bound is available.
claims.evidence: With r the minimum positive member size and T=Σ_A|A|=Σ_xd_x, the distinct canonical members X,M_1,…,M_{n−1} have respective lower sizes n and max(r,n−i). Separating them and ∅ from the other members gives T≥L, where L=n(n+1)/2+r(r−1)/2+r(m−n−1). This follows by exactly summing Σ_{k=1}^{n−1}max(r,k).
claims.search_method: Exact incidence double-count and canonical-size summation.

claims.claim: Frankl’s conjecture holds whenever the smallest positive member of the reduced family has size r≥n/2. In particular, it holds for every family with at most six inequivalent active elements.
claims.evidence: For the preceding L, exact simplification gives 2L−nm=(2r−n)(m−n−1)+r(r−1). Since m≥n+1, r≥n/2 implies T≥nm/2, so some frequency is at least m/2. Conversely a counterexample's reduced family can have no member of size one or two, so r≥3, while this result requires r<n/2. Therefore a counterexample needs n≥7, proving the six-class conclusion.
claims.search_method: Algebraic comparison of the incidence lower bound with nm/2.

claims.claim: A normalized separating counterexample with parameters n,m,r must have odd m and satisfy an explicit quantitative lower bound.
claims.evidence: For the normalized representative furnished by claims 0–2, m is odd. Every d_x≤(m−1)/2, so T≤n(m−1)/2. Combining this with L and using r<n/2 yields (n−2r)m≥n(n+2−2r)+r²−3r. Claim 5 also gives n≤(m−1)/2. Hence m≥max(2n+1, ceil((n(n+2−2r)+r²−3r)/(n−2r))), exactly the asserted quantitative restriction.
claims.search_method: Integer incidence upper/lower comparison after the odd-cardinality normalization.

claims.claim: Any normalized separating counterexample on seven elements must have at least 25 members.
claims.evidence: Here r=3 and the quantitative bound gives odd m≥21. For m=21, both incidence bounds equal 70, forcing all frequencies to be 10 and M_2={x_3,…,x_7}; then F_{x_1}⊆F_{x_2}, hence equality, contradicting separation. For m=23, 76≤T≤77. If M_2 has size five, separation forces d_1<d_2 and hence T=76; all remaining sets are triples, leaving at most X plus five triples containing {x_1,x_2}, contradicting d_1=10. If M_2=X\{x_2}, the unique excess is consumed; closure forces M_5={x_4,x_6,x_7} and M_6={x_4,x_5,x_7}. Fifteen further triples are needed, while union with M_3 restricts them to only 1+4+4+1=10 possibilities. The checker exhaustively confirms these finite subcases.
claims.search_method: Complete equality-case analysis plus exact enumeration of the remaining canonical-set and triple choices.

claims.claim: Frankl’s bound holds if the family is closed under both unions and intersections.
claims.evidence: Adjoin ∅ if absent and choose an inclusion-minimal nonempty A. For x∈A and any U avoiding x, U∩A is a proper member below A, so it must be ∅. Thus U is disjoint from A, and U↦U∪A injects members avoiding x into members containing x, with inverse deletion of A. This proves the augmented threshold and therefore the original one as well.

claims.claim: Exact enumeration verifies Frankl’s conjecture for every labelled ground set of size at most five and verifies the tight-clean power-set conclusion there.
claims.evidence: The checker decides subsets in nonincreasing size. Selecting S is allowed exactly when every already-determined union S∪T required by a selected T is present. At a leaf this ensures closure, while every union-closed family follows a unique branch, establishing completeness and no duplication. Counts for n=0,…,5 were 2, 4, 14, 122, 4960, and 2771104. There were zero eligible counterexamples. For each n=1,…,5 there was exactly one ∅-containing active separating tight family, and it was the full power set. A direct scan of all assignments independently matched every statistic through n=4.
claims.search_method: Exact exhaustive bit-mask generation, independently cross-checked by direct assignment enumeration through n=4.

claims.claim: The natural strengthening “every smallest nonempty member contains a Frankl element” is false.
claims.evidence: The persisted checker verifies 19 distinct members, all 361 ordered unions, minimum positive size three, and frequencies (9,9,9,14,14,14,17). Thus the smallest member {1,2,3} contains only elements of frequency 9, strictly below 19/2, while elements 4–7 are Frankl elements. This is a valid counterexample to the strengthening, not to Frankl’s conjecture.
claims.search_method: Exact integer bit-mask verification of distinctness, pairwise union closure, member sizes, and frequencies.
